claims.text: The initial as-cast Mg-containing lightweight HEA contains Mg-rich metastable solid-solution regions together with incipient intermetallic nuclei.
The proposed alloy is analogous to an Al-Mg-Cu-Zn-Gd alloy system.
Rapid solidification at at least 10^3 K/s and conventional induction-melting solidification at approximately 10 K/s will produce distinct microstructural states.
Cooling rate controls the relative retention of metastable phases and the nucleation and growth of stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Slow cooling permits diffusion-driven partial transformation of a metastable Mg-rich solid solution into discrete intermetallic precipitates.
Rapid cooling freezes in a higher fraction of the metastable Mg-rich solid solution.
The intermetallic precipitates act as preferential nucleation sites for oxide films.
Intermetallic-assisted oxide nucleation produces a more continuous and adherent protective film.
A protective passive film inhibits metal dissolution and improves aqueous corrosion resistance.
A continuous protective oxide film reduces the high-temperature oxidation rate.
Rapidly solidified material lacks the microstructural heterogeneities required for effective passivation.
Slow-cooled samples will have a lower corrosion current density than rapidly solidified samples.
Slow-cooled samples will have a lower cyclic high-temperature oxidation rate than rapidly solidified samples.
The comparison will use samples of identical alloy composition that differ in cooling history.
The proposed boundary conditions are cyclic oxidation in air at 700-900 °C and corrosion in 0.1 M H2SO4.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to lightweight alloys with density below 6 g/cm3.
Oxide morphology, continuity, composition, oxidation weight gain, and corrosion current density will be measured to test the mechanism.
The hypothesis is falsified if slow-cooled samples show no statistically significant reduction in both oxidation rate and corrosion current density relative to the rapidly solidified baseline.
